newsitem.title: DUBAI: Kuwait's allies uneasy over elections.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait's allies uneasy over elections.

text.p: Kuwait on Monday will elect the only Gulf Arab parliament in a region where states are uneasy with an outspoken chamber next door that probes scandals and puts the spotlight on alleged corruption.
"The Kuwaiti parliament is regarded as something alien. Other Gulf Arab states view it with varying degrees of suspicion," said a Western diplomat.
"They are uncomfortable with the whole political culture in Kuwait. It does not have a parallel anywhere else and they see the parliament as an implicit threat," he said.
Only some 107,000 men, about a seventh of Kuwaiti nationals, are allowed to vote to pick 50 new parliamentarians from 230 candidates seeking a seat in the sharp-tongued parliament.

The chamber has taken Kuwait closer to Western-style democracy than any other country in the Gulf, where ruling kings, emirs, sultans and sheikhs are coming under increasing pressure to give the people a greater say in politics.
Other Gulf states have appointed Shura councils, but the consultative bodies are virtually powerless, diplomats say.
"In most Gulf states there are the embryonic beginnings of processes of more political participation. But they are consultative and gifts of the rulers," said a Western expert on the Middle East.
The Kuwaiti parliament has become a more sensitive issue in the region, particularly in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain, according to analysts.

Saudi Arabia has come under attack from Moslem militants and exiled opposition groups who demand greater political participation and have accused the ruling family of alleged corruption and mismanagement of funds.
But even with two bomb attacks that killed 24 Americans and two Indians in the last year, the kingdom does not appear closer to introducing political reform, analysts say.

"The Saudi government is very sensitive to the elections in Kuwait. At the same time ordinary Saudis feel they are behind," said Saad al-Fagih, London-based leader of the Movement for Islamic Reform in Arabia.
"We would like a Saudi parliament in the future but if you had free elections next week nobody would know what to do. They would probably vote for the same ministers."
Bahrain will also be watching the Kuwaiti elections with a wary eye.
Shi'ite Moslems have waged a campaign of arson attacks, bombings and protests to demand reforms including the restoration of an elected parliament dissolved by the Manama government in 1975.
"The issue has an immediate sharpness for Bahrainis," said the Middle East expert.
Bahrain was angered in February when eight prominent Kuwaiti MPs wrote to its ruler, Sheikh Isa bin Sulman al-Khalifa, asking him to revive the parliament.
Elsewhere in the Gulf, there are signs that some countries are promoting change.
Independent-minded Qatar has said it plans to hold municipal elections next year, the first polls ever to be held in the country.
But analysts expressed doubt that the Gulf's political complexion would change in the near future.
"The other Gulf states are a long way behind Kuwait. The gap is pretty big," said the Middle East expert.
